Flood Insurance Data

Risk Rating 2.0

In FEMA's records, 44% of the 2,320,410 U.S. single-family primary-home NFIP policies with both premiums recorded pay a premium below FEMA's full-risk premium by any amount on August 31, 2026. Under Risk Rating 2.0, FEMA calculates premiums from the value of the home and the property's own flood risk. New NFIP policies beginning Oct. 1, 2021, and all policies renewing on or after April 1, 2022, are subject to it; a policyholder whose premium goes down moves to the lower rate at the first renewal.

44%
of 2,320,410 U.S. NFIP single-family primary-home policies: premium below FEMA's full-risk premium by any amount

FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Policies v3, as of August 31, 2026. The base is single-family primary-home policies in force with a premium (totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy) and a full-risk premium (fullRiskPremium) both above $0. Both are premium only, before fees and surcharges. How this is counted

How fast can a bill below full risk rise?

Some policies pay less than FEMA's full-risk premium because of discounts set by law. Except for the Emergency Program discount, those discounts shrink a little at each renewal, within the yearly cap on increases, until the policy reaches its full-risk premium.

By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year; the rate for some property, including homes that are not a primary residence and business property, rises 25% a year until that group's average rate reaches the level the law sets (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)). FloodSmart puts the limit at 18 to 25% a year for most policyholders. It usually does not apply to new policies, raising your coverage or lowering your deductible can go past it, and fees and surcharges are added on top.

What FEMA prices a policy on

FEMA prices each building from where it is (distance to the coast, rivers and other flood sources, and how high the ground sits), how it is built (foundation type, first-floor height) and what the policy covers (coverage amounts and deductibles).

The gap is FEMA's full-risk premium minus the premium charged, for each policy below full risk. A small median gap means most of those bills are close to full risk already. Your county page shows the county's share.

What this page cannot tell you

Your premium, your full-risk premium, when your bill will reach it, or why a price changed. FEMA's 2021 forecasts of who would pay more are not repeated here. These figures are the policies in force on August 31, 2026.
